title: The ENTIRE History of China in 16 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of China in 16 Minutes
description:
From the legendary Xia dynasty around 2070 BC to a six-year-old emperor stepping down in 1912, this is the whole story of imperial China: oracle bones, the First Emperor and his mercury pills, the Terracotta Army, the Silk Road, exam cells, the only woman emperor, gunpowder, paper money, Mongols, a giraffe for the Ming court, and the fall of the last dynasty. Every fact is checked against historians and museums, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #china #chinesehistory #animatedhistory #greatwall

beats.say: 210 BC. The most powerful man in the world has exactly one problem: he is going to die, and he would really rather not.
Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of China, has conquered every rival kingdom, and now he wants to conquer death itself.
Your Majesty, your daily immortality pill!
Excellent. What's in it this time?
Mercury, Majesty! Shiny, liquid, magical mercury!
Perfect. Make it a double.
Many historians think those mercury pills are probably what killed him, at just forty-nine years old.
The man who wanted to live forever was likely poisoned by his own immortality medicine. And that's just one weird chapter in four thousand years of Chinese history.
So grab some tea, because we're doing all of it: dynasties, dragon bones, a giraffe, and way too many walls.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of China in 16 Minutes

beats.say: Chinese tradition says it all starts with the Xia dynasty, around 2070 BC, founded by Yu the Great, a hero who tamed the great floods.
Here's the catch: nobody has ever found writing from the Xia, so historians still argue about whether it was a real dynasty, a legend, or a bit of both.
The first dynasty we can actually prove is the Shang, from about 1600 BC.
Shang kings made big decisions by asking their dead ancestors for advice, and the method was cracking bones.
Ancestors, will it rain tomorrow?
The crack says... maybe?
A priest carved the question into an ox shoulder blade or a turtle shell, heated it until it cracked, and the king read the cracks like a text from grandpa.
Those carvings, on what we now call oracle bones, are the oldest Chinese writing ever found.
In 1046 BC, the Zhou overthrew the Shang, and they explained why with a brand new idea: the Mandate of Heaven.
Heaven chooses who rules. Rule badly, and Heaven switches sides. Which is handy, because it means whoever wins was right all along.
Later, the Zhou kings lost control, and China split into rival states that fought for centuries, a stretch historians call the Warring States period.
In the middle of all that chaos, in 551 BC, a teacher named Confucius was born.
His big ideas: respect your family, be honest, study hard, and rulers should set a good example.

show.text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?

beats.say: He wasn't famous while he lived, but his students wrote down his sayings, and they shaped Chinese schools, families and government for more than two thousand years.
Then the state of Qin conquered its rivals one by one, and in 221 BC its king did something nobody had done before.
He united China and gave himself a shiny new title: Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor.
Then he standardized everything: one kind of writing, one set of weights, one coin, even one width for cart axles, so every wagon fit the same ruts.
He also joined up older walls in the north to keep out nomad raiders, an early ancestor of the Great Wall.
He could be ruthless, too. The old histories say he burned books and executed scholars who criticized him, though modern historians argue about how much of that is exaggerated.
And he was terrified of dying. He sent an alchemist named Xu Fu out to sea to find the elixir of life. Xu Fu never came back.
So the emperor planned for the afterlife instead.
In 1974, farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an hit something hard.
Uh, is this a pot?
Pots don't have mustaches.
They had found the Terracotta Army: thousands of life-size clay soldiers, plus horses and chariots, buried to guard the emperor's tomb.
The usual estimate is more than eight thousand soldiers, and parts of the site still haven't been dug up.

show.label: Terracotta soldiers (estimate)
show.sub: plus horses and chariots, and pits still unexcavated

beats.say: They were made almost like an assembly line, with heads from a handful of molds, then each face was finished by hand, so every soldier looks like his own person.
He had boasted that his dynasty would last ten thousand generations. After his death in 210 BC, it lasted four more years.

show.title: The Han and the Silk Road

beats.say: Next came the Han dynasty, which ruled for about four hundred years and was such a big deal that China's largest ethnic group still calls itself the Han.
In 138 BC, Emperor Wu sent an envoy named Zhang Qian west, to find allies against the Xiongnu, the nomads raiding the northern border.
He was captured by the Xiongnu almost immediately.
You're staying with us now.
For how long?
Oh, about ten years.
He escaped, finished the mission anyway, and came home after thirteen years with news of kingdoms nobody in China had heard of.
His journeys helped open the trade routes we now call the Silk Road, which carried Chinese silk west, all the way to the Roman Empire.
Rich Romans loved silk, and the Roman writer Pliny the Elder grumbled that luxuries from the East were draining the empire's money.
The Han also counted their people, and a census in the year 2 AD found more than fifty-seven million of them.
They also gave the world paper. The court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with it in 105 AD, but archaeologists have found older paper, so he probably improved it rather than invented it.
Then, in 220 AD, the Han fell apart, and China split into three rival kingdoms, then into centuries of division.
In 581, the Sui dynasty reunited China. It only lasted thirty-seven years, but it was busy.
The Sui linked up the Grand Canal between north and south, and in 605 they launched something that would outlive them by thirteen centuries: the imperial examinations.
The idea was that government jobs should go to whoever knew the most, not to whoever had the richest dad.
By later centuries, candidates memorized the Confucian classics, then got locked in a tiny cell for three days and two nights at a time to write their essays.
Three days in here? Where do I sleep?
The desk turns into a bed. You're welcome.
Of course people cheated, with tiny notes hidden in their clothes and brushes. Get caught, and you were thrown out.
The exams ran from 605 all the way to 1905, about thirteen hundred years.

show.label: China's imperial exams
show.sub: from 605 until they were abolished in 1905

beats.say: In 618, the Tang dynasty took over, and it's often called a golden age, with famous poets and a capital, Chang'an, that was one of the biggest cities on Earth.
And the Tang era produced the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own right: Wu Zetian.
She started as a low-ranking consort, became empress, helped run the government for her sickly husband, and then ruled through her sons.
In 690, she stopped pretending.
I'm not the emperor's mother anymore. I'm the emperor.
But Your Majesty, there's never been a woman emperor.
There is now.
She founded her own Zhou dynasty and ruled for fifteen years, until she was pushed out in 705, at around eighty.
Later historians painted her as a villain, but many modern scholars point out that her empire was stable and powerful, and she promoted officials through the exams.
Meanwhile, Tang alchemists were still chasing immortality, mixing saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal.
A Daoist text from around 850 warns that some of these mixtures burst into flames, burning people's beards and even their houses.
Well, it's not immortality. But it's definitely something.
That something was gunpowder.
The Tang collapsed in 907, and after a messy half century, the Song dynasty took over in 960.
The Song were basically the nerds of Chinese history, and I mean that as a compliment.
In Sichuan, people paid with iron coins, which were so heavy that buying a single bolt of silk could take dozens of kilos of them.
One bolt of silk, please.
Sure. Bring the wheelbarrow of coins around the back.
So merchants started trading paper receipts instead, and in 1024 the Song government took over and issued the world's first official paper money.
The Song also printed with movable type, invented by a craftsman named Bi Sheng in the 1040s, and by around 1100 Chinese sailors were steering by magnetic compass.
And gunpowder went from beard-burner to weapon: a military manual from 1044 contains the oldest known written gunpowder formulas.
Unfortunately for the Song, up north a man named Temujin had united the Mongol tribes, and in 1206 he took the title Genghis Khan.
The Mongols built the largest connected land empire in history, reaching from Korea into Eastern Europe, and in 1258 they sacked Baghdad.
His grandson Kublai Khan declared a new Chinese dynasty, the Yuan, in 1271, and finished off the Song by 1279.
Kublai tried to invade Japan twice, in 1274 and 1281, and both times storms helped wreck his fleets.
The wind is on our side!
Who invited the weather?
The Japanese called it kamikaze, the divine wind, though historians say the samurai defending the coast deserve plenty of credit too.
Also in 1271, a young Venetian named Marco Polo set out for Asia with his father and uncle.
He later claimed he served Kublai Khan for seventeen years. Some historians doubt he got that far, but plenty of his details check out.
Back home, he described paper money and enormous cities, and a lot of Europeans simply didn't believe him.
The Yuan lasted less than a century. In 1368, a rebel named Zhu Yuanzhang drove the Mongols out and founded the Ming dynasty.
His resume is wild: orphaned peasant, Buddhist monk, beggar, rebel general, and then emperor.
His son, the Yongle Emperor, moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City.
He also sent Admiral Zheng He across the Indian Ocean with hundreds of ships and more than twenty thousand men.
Between 1405 and 1433, his fleets reached India, Arabia, and the coast of East Africa.
In 1414, the Sultan of Bengal sent the emperor a gift that had originally come from East Africa: a live giraffe.
Long neck, hooves, gentle eyes. Is this a qilin?
Definitely a qilin, Majesty. Heaven clearly loves you.
The court hailed it as a qilin, a legendary creature said to appear only under a wise ruler. Great news for an emperor who had taken the throne from his own nephew.
But after 1433 the great voyages stopped, and the Ming turned inward.
Instead, they rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone, and most of the wall tourists visit today is Ming.
Add up every wall from every dynasty, and a 2012 survey measured over twenty-one thousand kilometers.
And no, you can't see it from the Moon with your naked eye. It's long, but only a few meters wide, and Apollo astronauts said no human-made object was visible from there. That one's a myth.
In 1644, rebels took Beijing, the last Ming emperor died, and the Manchus from the northeast swept in to found the Qing, China's last dynasty.
Under emperors like Kangxi and Qianlong, the Qing grew huge and rich.
In 1793, Britain sent Lord Macartney to ask for more trade, carrying fancy gifts like clocks and telescopes.
Your Majesty, behold, the finest British instruments!
Lovely. We have plenty.

show.text: As your Ambassador can see for himself, we possess all things.
show.who: Qianlong Emperor, letter to King George III, 1793 (trans. Backhouse and Bland)

beats.say: Britain wanted Chinese tea, but China didn't want much from Britain, so British merchants smuggled in opium from India to pay for it.
When China cracked down, Britain went to war. China lost the First Opium War, from 1839 to 1842, and had to hand over Hong Kong and open its ports.
Then came the Taiping Rebellion, led by a man who believed he was the younger brother of Jesus.
It lasted from 1850 to 1864, and historians estimate twenty to thirty million people died, making it one of the deadliest wars in human history.
By then the Empress Dowager Cixi held the real power at court, and the old system was cracking. In 1905, even the imperial exams were abolished.
In 1908, a two-year-old named Puyi became emperor, and according to his own memoir, he cried through the ceremony.
I don't want to be here! I want to go home!
In 1911, revolution broke out, and on February 12, 1912, six-year-old Puyi abdicated.
More than two thousand years of emperors began with a man who swallowed mercury to live forever, and ended with a little boy who just wanted to go home.
China's story kept going, of course, but that's where we stop today.
If you liked this, subscribe, because next up is The Weirdest Deaths in History, and yes, the mercury guy would fit right in.
